<full markdown: complete YAML frontmatter + body, per the AGENTS.md schema>
===END ARTICLE===

Use `connections/<slug>.md` for connection articles and `qa/<slug>.md` for Q&A.
Slugs are lowercase and hyphenated. To UPDATE an existing article, emit it with
its existing path and the full revised content (it overwrites).

After the article blocks, emit exactly one index block and one log block:

===INDEX===
| [[concepts/<slug>]] | one-line summary | 2026-09-27.md | 2026-09-27 |
===END INDEX===

===LOG===
## [2026-09-27T23:47:15-05:00] compile | 2026-09-27.md
- Source: daily/2026-09-27.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/<slug>]]
- Articles updated: (none)
===END LOG===

### Rules
1. Identify 3-7 distinct concepts worth their own article.
2. Emit ===NOTHING=== ONLY when the log itself contains no durable knowledge
   (e.g. "FLUSH_OK", or purely transient chatter). "An article already covers
   this topic" is NOT a reason to emit ===NOTHING=== - it is a reason to UPDATE
   that article with whatever this log adds.
3. Every article: complete YAML frontmatter (title, sources, created, updated)
   with `sources` citing 2026-09-27.md; at least 2 [[wikilinks]]; Key Points
   3-5 bullets; Details 2+ paragraphs; Related Concepts 2+ entries; encyclopedia
   style — neutral and comprehensive. Follow the AGENTS.md article format exactly.
4. Create a connection article when the log reveals a non-obvious relationship
   between 2+ concepts.
4b. Do NOT re-emit an article whose only change would be the `updated:` date or
   a restatement of what it already says. Measured on a real run, 4 of 5
   "updates" changed nothing but the timestamp - that is churn: it rewrites
   files, dirties backups, and invalidates caches while adding no knowledge.
   Re-emit an article only when you are adding substantive content.
5. Add one ===INDEX=== table row per article (new or updated).

Emit ONLY the delimiter blocks — no preamble, no commentary.

message.content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.


## Current Wiki Index

# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] | Adds 2026-07-09 GitHub MCP 401-on-reconnect: configured Authorization header disables OAuth fallback; fix is token refresh or header removal | 2026-06-10.md, 2026-04-14.md, 2026-06-03.md, 2026-06-09.md, 2026-07-09.md | 2026-08-01 |

# Course Video Download–Transcribe–Verify Pipeline (Sportsmith On-Field RTP)

On 2026-09-25, a Codex session ran a download → transcribe → verify → summarize pipeline over the Sportsmith course *Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation*, writing artifacts to `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\SS_Course_OnFieldRTP\Video Transcripts`. The session confirmed a dual-transcript verification workflow as the accepted standard for this course — an independently generated ASR transcript compared against the site-provided player captions, with a written comparison report — and ended partway through Part 4 at the user's request, leaving Part 5 unstarted. A later session the same day generalized the pipeline to a second course (see [[concepts/course-extraction-three-artifact-convention]]).

## Key Points

- **Dual-transcript verification is the accepted workflow:** each part gets a `yt-dlp` download, an independently generated ASR transcript, the site-provided player captions, a comparison report between the two, and a "checked" transcript derived from the comparison. This matches the prior session's practice and the existing `video-transcript-verification` skill.
- **Artifacts land in the `Video Transcripts` subfolder, not the parent course folder.** Video, captions, metadata, and raw ASR are saved per part; the standardization was made explicit after a stray Part 3 summary PDF was written to the parent `SS_Course_OnFieldRTP` folder.
- **Summary PDFs are not a deliverable here:** the course PDFs were already in hand, so generating or re-saving summary PDFs was ruled out.
- **A policy-blocked delete left the stray file in place.** The cleanup delete of the misfiled Part 3 summary PDF was refused by the permission layer, converting it into a manual user action rather than a completed fix.
- **Part status at session end:** Part 3 complete but carrying one flagged unclear injury term (no manual audio review performed); Part 4 has video, captions, metadata, and raw ASR saved but still needs the comparison, checked transcript, and summary; Part 5 not started.

## Details

The pipeline's distinguishing feature is that verification is built from two independent derivations of the same audio rather than from a single extraction plus human spot-checking. The site's player captions and a locally generated ASR pass are produced by different systems with different error profiles, so a diff between them localizes exactly where the text is uncertain — and the residue that survives comparison is the "checked" transcript. This directly addresses the known weakness of machine transcription established a day earlier during the Wistia course extraction, where the generated transcript was explicitly labeled a draft requiring cleanup before any staff-facing use (see [[concepts/wistia-course-video-extraction]]). The Part 3 outcome shows the method's honest limit: the comparison surfaced one injury term that neither source resolved, and rather than guessing, the term was flagged in the transcript with the absence of a manual audio review recorded alongside it.

Two operational lessons concern where output goes and who can clean it up. Because the course folder and its `Video Transcripts` subfolder are both plausible destinations, a summary PDF was written one level too high; the corrective rule adopted was to confirm the destination subfolder before writing rather than after. The attempted remedy then hit a second layer: the delete was blocked by policy, which is the same class of event as the Drive listing refused because athlete names appeared in file names (see [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]) — a guardrail behaving as designed, whose cost is an item that must be handed back to the user as a manual action instead of silently worked around. Both outcomes were carried forward as explicit action items (finish Part 4, process Part 5, manually delete the duplicate Part 3 PDF) rather than left implicit in the session's narrative.

By the afternoon of the same day the pipeline had been recognized as reusable rather than course-specific: a second course ("Sprint Biomechanics Fundamentals," Strength Coach Network) was run through the same extract → transcribe → summarize sequence in its own dedicated output folder, and the per-lesson deliverable was restated as a fixed three-artifact contract. The OnFieldRTP course's unfinished items (Part 4 comparison, Part 5, the stray PDF) were carried forward as open work alongside the new course rather than being closed out first.

# Claude Memory Compiler Setup

On 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` system — the same daily-log-to-knowledge-base architecture this very knowledge base runs on — was installed to give Claude Code persistent memory across sessions. The repo was cloned to `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/`, Python dependencies installed via `uv sync`, and the knowledge base directory structure (`daily/`, `knowledge/concepts/`, etc.) initialized. This system is Tier C of a three-tier Claude Code memory architecture; see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] for the full picture including Tier A (native auto-memory) and Tier B (custom Stop-hook scratchpad). On 2026-06-13, a day-long failure caused by `claude-agent-sdk` version skew revealed an important operational maintenance pattern.

## Key Points

- Three global hooks were wired into `~/.claude/settings.json`: `session-start.py` (SessionStart), `session-end.py` (SessionEnd), and `pre-compact.py` (PreCompact).
- Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`.
- All script invocations follow the `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler <script>` pattern, guaranteeing the correct virtualenv context regardless of the current working directory when a hook fires.
- Hook configuration changes are not picked up live — they require a full Claude Code restart (or a `/hooks` reload) before they take effect.
- After 6 PM local time, the `flush.py` background process automatically triggers `compile.py` to turn that day's daily log into knowledge articles, without manual intervention. Manual queries are also available via `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/query.py "<question>"`.
- **The agent itself never receives a "session ending" notification** — SessionEnd and PreCompact are harness-level events; the harness runs the hook shell commands, not the agent. Teardown logic must live in the hook, not in agent-side instructions.
- **Version skew failure mode:** the memory compiler's `uv` virtualenv pins `claude-agent-sdk` to a specific version, which bundles a specific Claude Code CLI binary. When the system Claude Code auto-updates (e.g., from 2.1.92 to 2.1.177), the bundled CLI in the venv falls behind and eventually cannot parse the current `~/.claude/settings.json`, causing every `flush.py` invocation to exit immediately with a non-zero code. Symptom: 100% FLUSH_ERROR rate after a Claude Code update, despite no changes to the memory compiler itself.
- **Fix for version skew:** `cd ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler && uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync`. This upgrades only the `claude-agent-sdk` dependency and its bundled CLI to match the current system version without touching other pinned dependencies. Run this whenever FLUSH_ERRORs appear after a Claude Code auto-update.
- **Diagnostic caution:** do NOT invoke the bundled `claude.exe` CLI directly to diagnose version skew — it spawns a real nested agent session. Instead, inspect venv package metadata (e.g., `uv pip show claude-agent-sdk`) to check the installed version against the system CLI version.

## Details

The setup session focused on making the memory pipeline reliable rather than merely functional. The PATH issue with `uv` is a generalizable lesson for any Claude Code hook that shells out to a tool installed via `uv`, `pipx`, or similar user-local installers: hook processes may run with a minimal environment, so absolute paths (or explicit `PATH` exports) are safer than relying on the interactive shell's configuration. Similarly, the `uv run --directory` pattern avoids a whole class of "wrong virtualenv" bugs that would otherwise occur if a hook fires while Claude Code's working directory is some unrelated project.

Once restarted, the three hooks form a closed loop: `session-start.py` injects the current knowledge index and the most recent daily log into every new session's context (capped at 20,000 characters), `session-end.py` and `pre-compact.py` capture the raw conversation transcript and spawn a detached `flush.py` process, and `flush.py` decides what's worth appending to the day's daily log and, after 6 PM, kicks off `compile.py` to synthesize that log into structured `knowledge/` articles. PreCompact serves as a safety net for long sessions: in a session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one, ensuring at least one compiled log exists even if the session later crashes before SessionEnd fires.

The 2026-06-13 version skew failure is operationally important. On that day, Claude Code auto-updated from approximately version 2.1.92 to 2.1.177 — 85 releases ahead — while the memory compiler's venv still bundled the older CLI via `claude-agent-sdk==0.1.56`. The newer `~/.claude/settings.json` included hooks, settings, or schemas added after version 2.1.92 that the stale bundled CLI could not parse; every `flush.py` call exited on startup without processing the session. The failure was isolated entirely to the Tier C compile layer: Tier B (the `transcript-capture.js` Stop-hook) continued capturing sessions uninterrupted because it has no dependency on `claude-agent-sdk`. Twenty-four days of continuous Tier B logs and four sessions captured on the failure day itself confirmed the architectural independence. This means that during a version-skew failure, raw session context is preserved in Tier B transcripts and can be backfilled after the fix is applied. The `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync` fix is surgical — it upgrades only the affected package without touching other pinned dependencies — and is safe to apply at any time. A post-fix test flush verifies the fix before trusting that normal operation has resumed. See [[connections/memory-compiler-tier-independence-under-failure]] for the architectural insight this failure demonstrated empirically.

- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — A later (2026-06-10) maintenance pass on the same Claude Code environment, addressing plugin/MCP configuration drift in the broader tooling this memory system runs inside.
- [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] — Another automation pipeline (built 2026-06-10) sharing the same token-efficiency motivation: pre-process inputs so the LLM only has to read a compact summary.
- [[connections/memory-compiler-tier-independence-under-failure]] — Documents the 2026-06-13 empirical demonstration that Tier B (transcript capture) remained fully operational through a day-long Tier C (compiler) failure, validating the architecture's independence claim under real failure conditions.

# Zotero API Integration Reference (Quirks and Gotchas)

Eight non-obvious Zotero API behaviors were identified and baked into the `zotero-research-library-pp-cli` HTTP client during Wave 4 of the tool's development on 2026-05-18. These quirks collectively make Zotero's API behave meaningfully differently from a naive REST-JSON assumption, particularly around sync versioning, write idempotency, partial-failure responses, and binary format passthrough.

## Key Points

- **`If-Modified-Since-Version` vs `since=N`:** the header is a conditional GET instruction ("return nothing if unchanged") and must NOT be auto-injected on batch fetches within an active sync run. Use the `since=N` query param exclusively for incremental sync; the header belongs only on requests where a 304 response is an acceptable no-op.
- **Write idempotency:** all write requests require a `Zotero-Write-Token` header (a client-generated idempotency token); repeat submissions of the same token are safely ignored by the server.
- **Partial-success writes:** the API returns a `MultiWriteResponse` when a batch write partially succeeds — some items created/updated, others rejected — requiring per-item inspection rather than treating the response as all-or-nothing.
- **Optimistic locking on writes:** a 412 Precondition Failed response indicates another client has written since the last read; the fix is to re-fetch the current `Last-Modified-Version` and retry the write with the updated version.
- **Format-specific response handling:** `format=keys`, BibTeX, and RIS responses must be passed through as raw bytes, not decoded as JSON; the HTTP client must detect these formats and skip JSON deserialization.
- **File-upload short-circuit:** the upload authorization endpoint may return `exists: 1`, meaning the file is already on the server and the byte-upload step should be skipped entirely.
- **403 vs 401:** 403 = Forbidden (access control issue, the credential is valid but lacks permission), 401 = Unauthenticated (bad or missing API key); these require different error-handling branches.

## Details

The `If-Modified-Since-Version` / `since=N` distinction is the most operationally dangerous quirk because a misapplication produces a silently successful-looking failure: the sync completes without error, but zero items are written. The header tells the Zotero server "return 304 and no body if nothing has changed since this version." In a sync run that starts by fetching the library's current version number (via `format=versions`), the locally stored version immediately updates to the current server version. If that version is then automatically sent as `If-Modified-Since-Version` on the subsequent batch-fetch calls in the same run, the server legitimately interprets this as "nothing has changed since the version I just told you about" and responds 304 — even though the client has never actually fetched the items. The `since=N` query parameter, by contrast, is an additive filter ("return only items modified after version N") and is safe to use within a sync run because it does not cause 304 short-circuiting. The practical rule: auto-injection of `If-Modified-Since-Version` in an HTTP client layer is always a mistake; the header must be set deliberately, only on requests where a 304 is an acceptable outcome.

The write-path quirks (write token, `MultiWriteResponse`, 412 retry) collectively reflect Zotero's multi-client, collaborative-library design. Unlike a simple single-user API where each write either succeeds or fails atomically, Zotero is designed for libraries that may be edited concurrently by multiple Zotero clients. The idempotency token prevents duplicate item creation if a write request is retried due to a network error. The partial-success response model means a single API call can have mixed results across the items in a batch. And the 412/optimistic-locking pattern ensures no client's write can silently clobber another's: the current library version must be known and asserted on every write, and any mismatch requires a read-then-retry cycle. This is significantly more complex than Catapult's or Perch's write models — see [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] and [[concepts/perch-api-integration-reference]] for comparison.

# Background Shell Jobs Reaped Under System Memory Pressure

On 2026-09-24, a long-running background job — a watch waiting for S2 data to appear on Google Drive — was terminated by Claude Code because the Windows laptop was critically low on memory. The termination was a resource-reclamation action, not a command failure, and the accompanying notification explicitly instructed that the job not be restarted. It was left dead, and the dependent check was reported as unconfirmed instead.

## Key Points

- **The harness may reap an idle session's background jobs to reclaim system memory.** The trigger is host memory pressure, independent of the job's own correctness or progress.
- **A reap notification is not a debugging signal.** There is no failing command to diagnose, no exit code to interpret, and no log to inspect — treating it as a bug wastes effort and invites a harmful retry.
- **Restarting on your own initiative is explicitly discouraged.** The notification carries that instruction, and relaunching the same memory-consuming watch on a host that just ran out of memory reproduces the condition that caused the kill.
- **The correct downstream behavior is to report the resulting gap.** With the watch gone, the S2 Drive state was simply unknown; the session recorded it as unverified rather than asserting or re-attempting a result.
- **Indefinite waits are the wrong shape for an in-session job.** A watch that blocks until an external event occurs has no bounded lifetime, making it the most likely candidate for reaping and a natural fit for a scheduled task instead.

## Details

Background-task notifications in Claude Code are ambiguous by default: the same channel reports genuine command failures, false-positive nonzero exits, and — as here — harness-initiated terminations. Distinguishing them matters because the correct response differs completely. A real failure calls for reading the log and fixing the cause; a false-positive exit calls for reconciling against on-disk artifacts, which is the lesson of [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]; a memory-pressure reap calls for doing nothing to the job and instead adjusting what is claimed downstream. The distinguishing evidence in this case was the notification's own text naming critically low memory and directing that the job not be restarted, which is a stronger signal than any exit code.

The structural lesson reinforces a limit already documented for this environment: work whose duration is unbounded does not belong inside a session. A watch waiting on an external filesystem event has no natural completion, so it accumulates the risk of session teardown, compaction, and — as seen here — resource reclamation, all of which kill it without completing the thing it was waiting for. The durable alternative is a scheduled job that polls and escalates on its own cadence, which is precisely the relocation applied to memsearch's hours-long reindex. In the immediate term, the session took the honest path: because the watch was the only mechanism that would have confirmed the S2 data landed on Drive, and a direct folder check was separately refused by the permission layer, the outcome was recorded as an unconfirmed item in the day's handoff rather than an assumed success.

- [[concepts/machine-split-workday-closeout]] — The closeout session in which this job was reaped and its unverified outcome carried forward as a named gap.

# Flush Selective Retention on Non-Working Sessions

The memory-compiler flush stage normally emits `FLUSH_OK` — writing nothing to the daily log — when a session produced no durable knowledge. The 2026-08-05 flush demonstrates a middle case: a session that was explicitly "a data snapshot, not a working session," with no decisions and no lessons, but whose contents were nonetheless preserved because several items carried hard deadlines or closing windows. The flush wrote the items down *and* annotated why, making the retention decision auditable rather than implicit.

## Key Points

- **Two distinct retention criteria.** The default criterion is *knowledge durability* (did this session teach something reusable?). The 2026-08-05 flush applied a second, orthogonal criterion: *time sensitivity* (will this item expire or escalate if not surfaced?). An item can fail the first test and still pass the second.
- **The retention rationale was written into the log itself.** The flush appended an explicit note — "This was a data snapshot, not a working session — no decisions or lessons produced. The action items above are preserved only because several are time-sensitive" — so a downstream reader (or compiler) knows the entry is a deliberate exception, not a misclassification.
- **Non-decision content is labeled as such.** The action items were headed "surfaced for follow-up, not new decisions," preventing the compiler from later mistaking a triage snapshot for a decision record.
- **What qualified as time-sensitive:** a security alert, a counterparty's closing availability window (leave dates), and immediate signature/confirmation actions. Ordinary aging replies were included only as context around these.
- **Cost trade-off:** preserving a snapshot costs a small amount of daily-log volume; discarding one risks dropping a deadline entirely, since the snapshot has no other durable home once the session ends.

## Details

The flush stage sits at a lossy boundary: it reads a session transcript and decides what, if anything, survives into `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Its default posture is aggressive discard, because most session chatter is transient and the daily logs are the compiler's source of truth. But a purely knowledge-oriented filter has a blind spot — operational obligations. A triage snapshot contains no lesson, no decision, and no reusable pattern, so it fails a strict "durable knowledge" test, yet it may be the only artifact in the system holding a 3-day-old security alert or a leave window that closes in three days. Once the session closes and the transcript is archived, that obligation has no other retrieval path.

The 2026-08-05 flush resolved this by widening the retention test rather than relaxing it: the items were kept under an explicitly named second criterion, and the reasoning was recorded inline. This self-documenting exception is the transferable practice. It avoids two failure modes at once — silently dropping deadline-bearing content, and silently inflating the log with snapshots that a future reader would mistake for substantive work. The pattern parallels the triage-vs-execution split seen in the inbox-triage runs themselves: surfacing and categorizing is a distinct act from deciding, and labeling output as one or the other keeps the downstream consumer honest. It also complements the broader principle behind the on-ramp pipeline — keep material retrievable while keeping the standing context lean — by admitting only the subset whose expiry cost justifies the space.

# Project Triage and Retrospective Methodology

On 2026-05-21, a structured 7-day retrospective (covering May 14–21) and a cold-project triage exercise were conducted to address project sprawl across many concurrent initiatives. The retrospective produced a structured cross-project summary of work completed and 7 open loops with next actions; the triage sorted cold projects into 4 buckets and shipped a decision-tracking HTML artifact at `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html`.

## Key Points

- **7-day retrospective format:** a structured recap of all projects touched in a rolling window, categorized by status, covering CLI development (Zotero, Catapult), 5 new skills installed, Fireflies setup, memory and Obsidian integration, token dashboard setup, and side fixes for May 14–21. Concluded with 7 identified open loops, each paired with a concrete next action.
- **Cold-project 4-bucket triage:** cold projects (not touched during the retrospective window) are sorted into: **Resume** (active work, blocked on a specific next action), **Decide** (uncertain whether to continue; needs a deliberate go/no-go decision), **Done** (formally closeable), **Archive/Kill** (permanently deprioritized or abandoned). The 2026-05-21 run sorted 16 projects: 3 resume, 2 decide, 3 done, 8 archive/kill.
- **Triage output artifact:** `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html` — a self-contained HTML file summarizing all bucketed projects with statuses and next actions, usable offline without re-running the triage.
- **Hottest cold project:** `Risk_Stratification_Engine` was flagged as the highest-priority cold project to resume next.
- **Project sprawl as a recurring pattern:** the user explicitly noted difficulty maintaining orientation across many concurrent initiatives; periodic retrospectives and triage dashboards were identified as the structural remedy.

## Details

The retrospective was triggered by the user explicitly losing track of what had been started, stopped, or left mid-flight — a common failure mode when many parallel workstreams run simultaneously across different tools, repositories, and roles. Rather than relying on memory or ad-hoc review, the session generated a structured cross-project summary covering the prior 7 days, making the "what exists and where it stands" question answerable in a single, deliberate pass. The format mirrors a lightweight sprint retrospective: scope (what was touched), status (done vs. in-flight vs. blocked), and open loops (concrete next actions, not vague intentions).

The 4-bucket triage model is designed to force explicit decisions rather than letting cold projects accumulate indefinitely in an ambiguous "maybe later" state. **Resume** identifies projects with a clear next action that are still worth pursuing. **Decide** surfaces projects that need a deliberate go/no-go call rather than being quietly ignored — the act of naming these forces a decision that passive neglect defers indefinitely. **Done** provides a formal closure signal for work that is genuinely complete but hasn't been officially closed. **Archive/Kill** handles deliberate deprioritization — not forgotten, but explicitly moved out of active consideration. The HTML artifact makes the triage durable and reviewable without accessing the session that produced it; sharing it as a file also separates the "what was triaged" question from the "what should I do next" question, allowing the artifact to be reviewed asynchronously.

The retrospective also surfaced a secondary benefit: completing deferred follow-up work from prior sessions. Specifically, the Zotero CLI's `sync --full` verification — left pending after the v0.1 slash command was registered on 2026-05-19 — was completed during the retrospective, with 2,064 items ingested successfully in ~75 seconds. Catching and completing loose ends like this is a natural output of a structured retrospective: open loops that were "almost done" become clearly visible and easy to close within the retrospective session itself.

- [[concepts/zotero-research-library-pp-cli]] — v0.1 was declared functionally complete during this retrospective after a successful `sync --full` run cleared the broken cached version left by the prior 304 bug.

- [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]] — Also designed on 2026-05-21, addressing the same "maintain orientation across many competing demands" problem at a daily cadence rather than a weekly retrospective cadence.

# Google Drive Cleanup via Antigravity CLI (agy)

On 2026-06-23, a Google Drive cleanup and organization session was run through the Antigravity CLI (`agy`), producing Python scripts to identify safe-to-delete shortcuts, quarantine duplicates for review, and pilot a content-based PDF rename workflow. The session established conservative, review-before-delete conventions and left an open gap around Google Keep authentication.

## Key Points

- **Safe-to-delete shortcuts = redundant paths only:** Drive symlink/shortcut files (curved-arrow icons) are safe to remove only when their target is also directly accessible elsewhere. Shortcuts that are the *sole* access path to a file must be kept. Scripts `detect_safe_to_delete_shortcuts.py` and `delete_safe_shortcuts.py` implement this distinction.
- **Quarantine duplicates, don't delete:** duplicates are moved to a "Mark for deletion" folder for human review rather than deleted outright (`move_duplicates_to_deletion.py`). Same-folder duplicates and cross-folder duplicates require separate detection logic.
- **Content-based PDF rename pilot:** a workflow extracts PDF content, proposes descriptive names, and stages them for review before committing (`pilot_rename_pdfs.py`, `generate_rename_proposal.py`, `pdf_extracts.json`), with `proposed_renames.md` and `pilot_rename_results.md` as review artifacts.
- **Google Keep auth gap:** a provider/auth prompt was encountered when attempting Keep access; the user had no provider name handy and moved on. Keep integration remains unconfigured for any future session that wants it.
- **agy-to-memory bridge intent:** the user confirmed they want all `agy` (Antigravity CLI) conversations captured in their memory infrastructure, extending the memory-capture net beyond Claude Code sessions.

## Details

The session's governing principle was conservatism around destructive operations: at every decision point, the chosen approach preserved reversibility. Shortcuts were classified by whether removing them would lose access to a file — only truly redundant shortcuts (where the target remains reachable) were marked safe to delete. Duplicates were never deleted directly; instead they were relocated to a dedicated "Mark for deletion" folder so the user could review the full set before any permanent removal. This mirrors the safe-deletion discipline seen elsewhere in the user's tooling, such as verifying an empty `.git` folder before deletion in [[concepts/accidental-git-init-home-directory]].

The PDF rename pilot follows a three-stage extract → propose → review pattern structurally identical to other content-transformation workflows the user favors: extract source content, generate descriptive proposals, and stage them in a reviewable markdown artifact before committing at scale. This is the same architecture as the Fireflies batch-rename workflow (propose, confirm, apply) documented in [[concepts/fireflies-batch-rename-workflow]], applied to Drive PDFs instead of meeting titles. Two open items constrain the session's completion: the Google Keep provider/auth was never resolved (a gap if Keep integration is later wanted), and the user's stated intent to bridge `agy` conversations into their memory infrastructure needs confirmation that capture is actually occurring. The multi-script decomposition (separate scripts for same-folder vs. cross-folder duplicates, detection vs. deletion) reflects a deliberate separation of read/analysis operations from write/destructive operations, keeping each script's blast radius small.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/fireflies-batch-rename-workflow]] — The same extract/propose/confirm/apply rename pattern applied to meeting titles; both workflows stage proposals for review before applying changes at scale.
- [[concepts/accidental-git-init-home-directory]] — Shares the "verify before destructive action" discipline; both confirm that removal will not lose data before proceeding.
- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The memory infrastructure the user wants `agy` conversations bridged into; extending capture to a non-Claude-Code tool (Antigravity CLI) is a new ingestion source for the same tiered memory system.

# Fireflies CLI Name-Based Search and Vault Ingest

On 2026-06-25, the `fireflies-pp-cli` was used to resync the local Fireflies cache and locate/ingest all meetings involving a named participant ("Danny Davis") into the SecondBrain vault. The session established that `--participant` matches on email only (unreliable for name search) while `--keyword` is the correct flag for name-based searches, that the local cache can silently go stale, and that CLI-exported notes require manual patching to conform to the vault's meeting-note template.

## Key Points

- **`--participant` is email-only; use `--keyword` for names:** `fireflies-pp-cli --participant` matches against participant email addresses, not names, making it unreliable for name-based lookups. `--keyword` (matching title/summary and other text fields) is the correct flag for finding meetings by a person's name.
- **Local cache can silently go stale:** the local Fireflies cache had 0 transcripts synced (only channels/users), so local search would have returned nothing. A full resync (196 transcripts, matching the live API) was required before trusting local results — always check sync state first.
- **Full-field sweep confirmed a single genuine match:** sweeping title, gist, overview, action items, and keywords confirmed exactly one genuine "Danny Davis" meeting (`DannyDavis_Call_04222026`, Apr 22 2026); a second "Danny" hit was a false positive (unrelated equipment staff).
- **Upstream transcript loss:** 3 of 5 transcripts missing cached summaries returned "Transcript not found" on the live API — likely deleted/expired upstream and not recoverable.
- **CLI export doesn't match the vault template:** `fireflies-pp-cli transcripts export` emits only Date/Status/Summary; the exported note had to be manually patched to add the vault's standard sections (Project tags, Key topics, Decisions, Action items, Open questions).

## Details

The session surfaced three distinct reliability considerations for CLI-driven meeting search and ingest. First, flag semantics: `--participant` performs email-only matching, which fails for name-based queries because a search for "Danny Davis" will not match unless the exact email is known. The `--keyword` flag, which matches against text fields including title and summary, is the correct tool for name search — but it also requires a full-field sweep (title, gist, overview, action items, keywords) plus human disambiguation to separate a genuine match from a false positive, as happened here when a second "Danny" turned out to be unrelated equipment staff. Second, cache freshness: the local Fireflies cache had silently desynced to 0 transcripts (retaining only channels/users), so any local search would have returned empty. A full resync producing 196 transcripts (matching the live API count) was the prerequisite to trusting local results — reinforcing the stale-cache gotcha already documented for the batch-rename workflow.

Third, ingest-format mismatch: the CLI's `transcripts export` command produces a minimal note (Date/Status/Summary) that does not conform to the SecondBrain vault's meeting-note template, which expects Project tags, Key topics, Decisions, Action items, and Open questions sections. Bridging this gap required manual patching of the exported note. The session also encountered a broken tool dependency — the `everything-search` skill is missing its `scripts/search.py` at `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\everything-search` and is non-functional on this machine; the vault path (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain`) was instead located via `data/memory-sources.json` in the KeystoneOS repo. Two follow-ups were logged: repairing/reinstalling the `everything-search` skill, and considering whether `transcripts export` should emit the full vault template by default to eliminate manual patching on future ingests.

- [[concepts/secondbrain-vault-infrastructure]] — The vault the meetings are ingested into; its plain-markdown meeting-note template (Project tags, Key topics, Decisions, Action items, Open questions) is the format the CLI export had to be manually patched to match.

- [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] — Checking the local cache sync state (0 transcripts) against the live API (196 transcripts) before trusting search results is a direct application of verifying against the authoritative source rather than the intermediate cache.

# Claude Code Three-Tier Memory Architecture

The Claude Code memory system is composed of three independent layers, each operating at a different granularity and owned by a different mechanism. This architecture was articulated on 2026-05-19 during a session that traced exactly when and how each capture mechanism fires, and clarified several non-obvious details about hook timing and agent visibility. On 2026-06-05, a practical capacity-management routing pattern emerged for when Tier B global memory approaches its character cap.

## Key Points

- **Tier A — Native Claude Code auto-memory:** Built into Claude Code itself; managed per-project; no user configuration required. Operates automatically within a project context; its exact retention and synthesis mechanics are not user-visible.
- **Tier B — Custom global scratchpad via Stop hook:** A user-configured hook on the `Stop` event, which fires after every conversation turn. This provides incremental, per-turn transcript capture to a global scratchpad file (MEMORY.md) — a granularity that neither Tier A nor Tier C provides.
- **Tier C — claude-memory-compiler:** The [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] system: `SessionEnd` and `PreCompact` hooks fire shell commands at session teardown or auto-compaction, spawning a detached `flush.py` process that appends structured notes to the daily log; at end-of-day these are compiled into knowledge articles.
- **The agent never sees a "session ending" event.** Session end and compaction are harness-level events; it is the Claude Code harness that runs the hook shell commands, not the agent itself. This means an in-context agent cannot intercept or react to its own termination — only the hooks can.
- **PreCompact as a safety net:** In a long session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one. If a session later crashes before `SessionEnd` fires, at least one Tier C log was written at the most recent compaction — preventing total context loss.
- **When Tier B is near cap, route to Tier A project files:** The global MEMORY.md (Tier B) has a character-cap constraint. When it approaches capacity, new durable facts should be saved to Tier A project-specific memory files (e.g., `project_<name>.md`, `user_career_timeline.md`) rather than forcing compression of existing Tier B entries. Tier A project files are cross-project searchable via memsearch — they are not siloed to a single project context.

## Details

The three tiers are designed to capture context at different time horizons and granularities, and they operate independently rather than hierarchically. Tier A is fully opaque to the user — Claude Code manages it internally on a per-project basis. Tier B's Stop-hook scratchpad is the most granular: because the Stop event fires after every conversation turn, Tier B can capture mid-session context incrementally in near-real-time. This is especially useful for long sessions where intermediate turns might be compacted away before Tier C's end-of-session capture fires. Tier C produces the richest synthesized output — compiled knowledge articles from daily logs — but fires only at session boundaries.

The independence of the three tiers is their key reliability property. A failure in one does not cascade to the others: if a session crashes before `SessionEnd` fires (blocking Tier C's flush), the Stop-hook's Tier B scratchpad may still contain the session's important turns. If the Stop hook misfires, Tier A's native memory and Tier C's PreCompact-triggered captures are unaffected. The "agent never sees session ending" detail is architecturally important for anyone building on top of these hooks: code written inside the agent context cannot detect or react to its own session ending. Teardown logic must be placed in hook shell commands that the harness executes, not in agent-side instructions. This distinction separates what the LLM can do (respond to turns, use tools) from what the harness can do (run shell commands on system events like session end, compaction, or turn completion).

The Tier B near-cap routing pattern (2026-06-05) addresses a practical capacity constraint that emerges over time as the global MEMORY.md accumulates active threads. The USER.md profile has a hard 1,375-character cap (documented in [[concepts/end-of-day-structured-interview]]), and MEMORY.md's Tier B can similarly fill as a productive user's open questions and active threads accumulate across weeks. The correct response when Tier B is near capacity is not to compress existing entries — which risks discarding information encoded in current phrasing — but to route new durable facts into named Tier A project memory files. These files are typically named per relationship or project (e.g., `project_kenny_boyd.md` for facts about a key stakeholder, `user_career_timeline.md` for career-context facts that help future sessions orient quickly) but are surfaced by memsearch across all project contexts. Routing to Tier A therefore sacrifices no cross-project retrievability while relieving pressure on the shared Tier B capacity. Facts that belong in Tier A project files are those that are both durable (will not become stale quickly) and specific enough that they do not need to live in the global scope — as opposed to cross-cutting facts about user preferences or universal workflow patterns that genuinely belong in Tier B's global scope.

# Fireflies Meeting Batch Rename Workflow

A Fireflies meeting batch rename workflow identifies meetings with generic timestamp-only titles, proposes descriptive names based on meeting content (gist) and participants, confirms with the user, and applies the renames via the Fireflies API (invoked through the `name-meetings` skill or the `fireflies_update_meeting_title` MCP tool). On 2026-06-17, 35 meetings were scanned; 6 were stale-cache false positives and 8 were genuinely renamed. On 2026-06-23, a follow-on batch of 10 (Jun 16–17) was proposed. On 2026-06-24, a two-batch run (30-day then expanded 180-day lookback) renamed 10 meetings, queued 22 more, and surfaced token-efficiency, MCP-reliability, and auto-mode-classifier hazards. On 2026-06-25, a related name-based search-and-ingest task confirmed the `fireflies-pp-cli` flag semantics and cache-freshness discipline underlying the workflow.

## Key Points

- **Workflow steps:** (1) invoke the rename skill/tool and confirm auth, (2) sync/scan Fireflies meetings from a rolling window, (3) identify generic or timestamp-only titles, (4) propose descriptive names from the meeting gist and participants, (5) confirm proposed names with the user before applying, (6) apply renames via the Fireflies API, (7) re-sync the local DB.
- **`--participant` is email-only; use `--keyword` for name search (2026-06-25):** `fireflies-pp-cli --participant` matches participant email addresses, not names. For finding meetings by a person's name, `--keyword` (matching title/summary text) is the correct flag.
- **Haiku gist-pull token strategy:** gist JSONs are multi-KB each, so pulling them with Haiku subagents (and trimming output to the `gist` field only) keeps token cost down on large batches.
- **Lookback windows scale by need:** a 30-day window catches recent accumulation; an expanded 180-day window surfaces older backlog (22 additional generic-titled meetings found on 2026-06-24).
- **Stale local cache gotcha:** the local Fireflies DB retains prior-session records and may report already-renamed meetings as "generic" — or silently desync to 0 transcripts entirely (2026-06-25). Re-verify sync state and re-check against the live Fireflies API before trusting local results.
- **Personal recordings surface alongside work meetings:** Fireflies captures non-work recordings (e.g., 4 church-sermon recordings on 2026-06-24) that must be separated out for explicit user confirmation rather than silently renamed.

## Details

The batch rename workflow addresses accumulation of AI-generated meeting notes with unnavigable timestamp titles. Converting these to descriptive, topic-oriented titles makes the meeting corpus searchable by subject and improves downstream knowledge-graph quality, since graphify extracts clearer entity and community labels when source filenames reinforce the meeting topic. The 2026-06-24 run demonstrated a two-tier lookback cadence: a first 30-day scan (35 meetings → 10 generic → all 10 renamed) followed, at user request for a deeper sweep, by a 180-day expansion that surfaced 22 more generic-titled meetings. Because gist JSONs are large, the token-efficient approach is to pull gists with cheap Haiku subagents and trim the response to only the `gist` field before proposing titles.

Three operational hazards were characterized on 2026-06-24. First, **MCP mid-session disconnects** are a real hazard for multi-batch runs: the Fireflies MCP connection can drop between batches, so connectivity must be re-checked before starting a second batch. Second, the **auto-mode classifier can false-positive**: it flagged a Fireflies MCP reconnect message (injected as system context) as a potential prompt injection and blocked the Haiku subagent spawns, forcing a fallback to direct gist pulls. The subagent pattern is sound and should be retried once subagent permissions stabilize. Third, the **Fireflies CLI `transcripts update` command has a known bug** (wrong field name); the reliable path is the MCP `fireflies_update_meeting_title` tool rather than the CLI. Finally, personal recordings such as church sermons appear in Fireflies alongside work meetings and must be surfaced separately for explicit user confirmation — on 2026-06-24, 18 of 22 queued meetings were work meetings and 4 were church-sermon recordings held pending user approval. The 2026-06-25 name-search session reinforced the cache-freshness discipline underlying all Fireflies CLI work: the local cache had silently desynced to 0 transcripts and required a full resync (to 196, matching the live API) before any search could be trusted, and confirmed the `--participant` (email-only) vs `--keyword` (name-search) flag distinction; see [[concepts/fireflies-cli-name-search-vault-ingest]] for the full name-search-and-ingest workflow.

# Permission Layer Blocking Athlete-Data Verification

On 2026-09-24, a direct check of the S2 data folder on Google Drive was refused by Claude Code's permission layer because the directory listing itself included an athlete-named file. No workaround was attempted; the session reported the block, told the user that a permission rule would be needed to allow such confirmations in future, and recorded the migration's landing state as unconfirmed. The episode is a clean example of an athlete-data guardrail working as designed while imposing a real verification cost.

## Key Points

- **A filename can be the protected content.** The block was triggered not by reading a file's contents but by *listing* a directory, because athlete names appear in the file names — so directory metadata is itself identifiable data under the policy.
- **No circumvention was attempted.** Rather than rerouting through a different tool, a shell glob, or a partial listing, the refusal was accepted and surfaced. Guardrails around athlete and health data are treated as policy, not as obstacles to engineer around.
- **The remedy is an explicit permission rule, not an ad-hoc override.** The user was told that allowing future confirmations requires adding a rule — a deliberate, reviewable configuration change rather than a one-off bypass.
- **The cost is a verification gap, and the gap must be named.** Combined with the same session's reaped background watch, the block left no path to confirm the S2 data had landed on Drive; the outcome was carried into the handoff as unconfirmed rather than assumed.
- **This is the enforcement surface of an existing policy.** The destination-split rule already routes athlete-identifiable data to Drive only and never to GitHub; the permission layer is where that intent becomes mechanical.

## Details

The interesting property of this block is where the sensitivity lives. Most data-governance rules assume the payload is the risk and the path is neutral, which is why gitignoring a `data/` directory is usually sufficient — the files stay out of the remote, and naming them is harmless. Here the inverse held: the request was a listing, the payload was never read, and the identifiable information was carried entirely in the file names. Any tool that enumerates a directory therefore handles athlete-identifiable data, which means the guardrail has to sit at the enumeration boundary rather than only at the read boundary. That is broader than it first appears and explains why an apparently innocuous `ls`-equivalent triggered a refusal.

The response pattern is the transferable part. A blocked operation creates pressure to find an equivalent path — a different tool, a narrower glob, a count instead of a listing — and each of those would technically satisfy the request while defeating the rule's purpose. Declining to look for one, and instead escalating to "a permission rule would be needed," keeps the decision with the person who owns the policy and leaves an auditable record of what was and was not verified. The cost is accepted honestly: the S2 Drive confirmation simply did not happen, and because the background watch that would otherwise have reported the arrival was reaped for memory pressure in the same session, the item left the day as an explicit unknown. An unconfirmed item in a handoff is a better artifact than a confident claim produced by working around a guardrail.

# OKR Tracker CLI (okr-tracker/okr.py)

On 2026-06-01, a lightweight Python CLI OKR tracker was built at `okr-tracker/okr.py` to support the [[concepts/applied-performance-okr-system]]. The tool reads YAML OKR data and generates a scoreboard markdown file, operating with zero external dependencies beyond PyYAML — a deliberate design choice driven by the SecondBrain vault's no-community-plugins constraint and IT policy restrictions on scheduled automation.

## Key Points

- **YAML data + generated scoreboard markdown:** OKR state (objectives, key results, confidence scores, ownership) lives in a YAML file; the CLI generates a readable markdown scoreboard on demand.
- **Dependency-light by design:** PyYAML-only on Python 3.14 (PyYAML 6.0.3 already available in Eric's environment) — no Dataview, no database, no web framework.
- **Plugin-free:** deliberately avoids Obsidian Dataview or any community plugin dependency, consistent with the vault's plain-markdown design (see [[concepts/secondbrain-vault-infrastructure]]).
- **Seed confidence numbers:** the initial YAML data was seeded with estimated confidence values; Eric noted these may need adjustment if estimates feel off after review.
- **No scheduler:** the CLI is run on demand; no cron job or automated scheduler was configured due to IT policy constraints — the same constraint that kept the vault's `backup.sh` manual.

## Details

The design philosophy of the OKR tracker is minimum viable tooling: a YAML file provides human-readable, version-controllable OKR state; a Python script reads it and outputs a formatted markdown scoreboard. This approach avoids the dependency chain of Obsidian community plugins — specifically Dataview, which is the natural plugin-based solution for dynamic OKR dashboards in Obsidian — and is consistent with the SecondBrain vault's intentional plain-markdown-only constraint. Because the generated scoreboard is a standard markdown file, it can be placed directly inside the vault and read without any special rendering or plugin support.

The YAML-plus-script pattern is also portable: the tracker data and generator script live in `okr-tracker/` as a standalone directory, independent of the vault's internal structure. This separation means updates to the tracker (adding new fields, changing scoreboard layout, adding trend data) do not require touching vault notes directly. The trade-off is that scoreboard updates are not automatic — the CLI must be run explicitly to refresh the generated file — but for a Thursday-cadence check-in workflow, on-demand generation is sufficient. The IT policy constraint prohibiting cron schedulers reinforces this design choice by making on-demand execution the only viable path. See [[connections/vault-constraints-shape-tooling-design]] for how this constraint propagated from vault infrastructure into both this tracker and the vault's backup script.

# Project Docs File-Map Pattern: API Surfaces in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md

On 2026-05-28, a "Simulator file map" section was added to the Baylor Load Simulator's `AGENTS.md`, documenting the exported API surfaces of `SimulatorClient.tsx`, `loadCalc.ts`, and `syncPractice.ts`. The intent is to let future sessions answer "what does this file export and how do I call it?" directly from the project docs, without opening and re-reading the source file — reducing context-window cost and speeding up session start-up when returning to an established codebase.

## Key Points

- A **file map section** inside `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` lists, for each key source file: the file path, its primary exports (component name, function signatures, type definitions), and usage notes (props, required arguments, return values, side effects).
- The pattern targets files that are called frequently across sessions but rarely change structurally — candidate files are the "integration points" of a codebase: API clients, calculation libraries, sync orchestration functions.
- On 2026-05-28, three Baylor Load Simulator files were documented this way: `SimulatorClient.tsx` (the React client component's prop interface), `loadCalc.ts` (the load calculation function signature and parameters), and `syncPractice.ts` (the sync orchestration entry point and its options shape).
- This pattern is additive to the `@AGENTS.md` import stub approach (see [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]]): the stub ensures Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md`, and the file-map section inside `AGENTS.md` provides the symbol-level detail that makes re-reading source files unnecessary in routine sessions.
- The file-map section belongs under a clearly labeled heading (e.g., `## Simulator file map`) and should be updated whenever a documented API surface changes — treating it as live documentation rather than a one-time snapshot.

## Details

The context-window cost of re-reading source files in each session is non-trivial for an established codebase: a single read of `SimulatorClient.tsx` to locate a component's prop interface may consume hundreds of tokens and require the session to read several hundred lines of JSX before reaching the relevant export. A file-map entry for the same component — two to five lines listing the prop names, types, and defaults — answers the question in under 50 tokens. Across a session that touches three or four integration points, the accumulated savings can shift a modest portion of the context budget toward productive work rather than orientation.

The pattern works best for files with stable, narrow, well-defined API surfaces: data-model classes, utility functions, API client adapters, and calculation libraries are good candidates; broad page components with many internal sub-components, or files under active refactoring, are poor candidates (the map would go stale quickly). A practical heuristic: if a file has been read by the assistant in two or more consecutive sessions primarily to look up a function signature or a component's expected inputs, it belongs in the file map. The file-map section should list only the exported API surface — not implementation details, not internal helper functions — so that it remains a concise lookup index rather than an inline copy of the source. When a documented file is substantially refactored, updating the file-map entry is the same category of maintenance task as updating a `CLAUDE.md` known-gotchas section: a few minutes of documentation work that pays dividends across many future sessions.
