## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. # Force Plate Practitioner Course Archive and Zotero Import

On 2026-09-27, the Force Plate Practitioner course (an Applied Performance community course) was archived to Google Drive and its associated reading list imported into Zotero, closing out a project carried over from a prior Codex session. The archive comprises 76 videos across 14 sections — each with the standard three-artifact deliverable — plus 9 course PDFs, 8 saved articles, and a resource catalog, all under `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\Force_Plate_Practitioner\`. A 52-record RIS package was imported into Zotero, and the scope was declared substantially complete with Flint ingestion tracked as a separate follow-up.

## Key Points

- **Scale and structure:** 76 lessons × 3 artifacts = 228 lesson files across 14 sections, following the established per-lesson contract (MP4 + checked transcript + summary), with all output under one dedicated course folder.
- **Supplementary materials archived alongside video:** 9 course PDFs, 8 saved articles, and a resource catalog were captured, making the folder the single destination for the course rather than splitting media from readings.
- **Zotero import via file association:** the 52-record `Force_Plate_Practitioner_New_Items_with_PDFs.ris` was imported by running `Start-Process` on the `.ris` file, which opens Zotero's import dialog through the Windows file association.
- **Collection mismatch resolved by renaming, not re-importing:** the import landed in an auto-created collection instead of the intended `APC_JumpsCourse`; the collection was renamed to "Force Plate Practitioner" rather than moving items or re-running the import, avoiding duplicate records.
- **Verification performed at completion:** the renamed collection was confirmed at 52 items, all 9 PDFs confirmed present and hash-matched against their Drive originals, and the research connector was confirmed able to read a page from a course PDF.
- **Explicit QA caveat:** the transcript labels claim caption-vs-ASR comparison only, not a full manual audio review; summary claims and cited studies were not independently validated.

## Details

The archive is the third and largest course run through the course-extraction pipeline, following the Wistia extraction on 2026-09-24 and the Sportsmith On-Field RTP and Sprint Biomechanics runs on 2026-09-25. Its scale — 76 lessons rather than a handful of parts — is what makes the three-artifact convention pay off: a fixed per-lesson deliverable gives an unambiguous denominator (228 files expected) and turns completion into an arithmetic check rather than a judgment call. The same session that confirmed the count also stated the QA boundary plainly: "checked" here means the ASR pass was diffed against vendor captions, nothing more. Neither a manual audio review nor validation of the summaries' factual claims and cited studies was performed, so the archive's transcripts carry the same draft-plus-cross-check status established in the earlier runs, and its summaries carry no verification at all. Stating that boundary alongside the delivery count is what keeps a large "complete" claim honest.

The Zotero half of the session produced the more transferable operational knowledge. RIS import on Windows is only semi-headless: `Start-Process` on the `.ris` file opens the import dialog, but a human must confirm it, and the dialog's "create new collection" checkbox is enabled by default — which is exactly why the 52 records landed in an auto-created collection rather than `APC_JumpsCourse`. The chosen remedy was the cheaper and safer one: rename the collection that already held the correct records, rather than move them or re-import into the intended collection and risk duplicates. That the rename then succeeded programmatically through Zotero's local API, after a coincidental Zotero update, is what produced the session's main API finding (see [[concepts/zotero-local-api-write-support]]). One residual constraint was noted: the 9 PDFs are attached as linked files living in Google Drive, and Zotero does not sync linked files through its own file storage — so the attachments' durability depends on Drive, not on Zotero. Flint ingestion of the same PDFs was left unverified and deliberately carved out as a separate follow-up rather than allowed to block the close-out.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/course-extraction-three-artifact-convention]] — The per-lesson deliverable contract this archive instantiates at 76-lesson scale; the declared inventory supplies the completion denominator.
- [[concepts/course-video-transcript-verification-pipeline]] — The download → transcribe → verify → summarize pipeline whose caption-vs-ASR comparison produced this course's "checked" transcripts, with the same manual-audio-review caveat.
- [[concepts/zotero-local-api-write-support]] — The Zotero 9 read-only / Zotero 10 writable local API finding that emerged from this session's collection rename.
- [[concepts/zotero-research-library-pp-cli]] — The existing Zotero tooling in this environment; this import was done through the desktop client's RIS dialog rather than through the CLI.
- [[concepts/dev-github-drive-migration-policy]] — Governs why professional-development course media lives under `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` rather than in a repository.
- [[connections/declare-the-output-contract-before-the-batch]] — Why a fixed per-lesson spec makes a 228-file delivery verifiable.

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-09-27.md]] — Force Plate Practitioner archiving session (23:47): 76 videos / 228 lesson files / 14 sections plus 9 PDFs, 8 articles and a resource catalog; 52-record RIS import via `Start-Process`; auto-created collection kept and renamed; 52 items, 9 hash-matched PDFs and research-connector read verified; linked-file sync caveat; transcript QA scope caveat; Flint ingestion deferred.

# Zotero Local API Write Support (v9 Read-Only, v10 Writable)

Zotero's local HTTP API is read-only in version 9.x; write support begins in Zotero 10. This was established on 2026-09-27 while trying to reorganize a freshly imported collection during the Force Plate Practitioner course archiving session: programmatic writes were impossible until a coincidental Zotero update crossed the version boundary, after which a collection rename succeeded through the local API. The finding removes a standing blocker on automated Zotero work in this environment.

## Key Points

- **Version boundary:** Zotero 9.x exposes a read-only local API; Zotero 10 adds local write support (documented at `zotero.org/support/dev/web_api/v3/local_api`). No setting makes a v9 local API writable.
- **The "Allow other applications" toggle is about access, not writes.** Enabling it in Zotero's settings permits local API *access*; it does not grant write capability on v9, so it is not the fix for a failing write.
- **RIS import on Windows is not fully headless.** `Start-Process <file>.ris` opens Zotero's import dialog via the file association but requires GUI confirmation. A genuinely terminal-driven import needs a write-enabled Zotero **Web** API key instead.
- **The import dialog defaults to creating a new collection.** The "create new collection" checkbox must be unchecked in the dialog to route records into a pre-selected collection; leaving it checked silently produces a stray collection.
- **Linked-file attachments do not sync through Zotero file storage.** PDFs attached as linked files (e.g. living in Google Drive) are outside Zotero's sync, so their durability and portability depend on the host filesystem, not on Zotero.

## Details

The practical shape of this finding is that Zotero offers two distinct programmatic surfaces with different capability profiles, and picking the wrong one produces a dead end that looks like a permissions problem. The local API is convenient — no key, no network, no rate limits — but on v9 it can only read, so any automation that must create, rename, or move records fails regardless of how the client is configured. The natural but incorrect diagnostic move is to hunt through Zotero's settings for a write toggle; "Allow other applications to communicate with Zotero" appears to be that toggle and is not, because it gates access rather than mutation. The correct resolution is either to upgrade to Zotero 10, where local writes are supported, or to fall back to the Zotero **Web** API with a write-enabled key — the same API surface whose write-path quirks (write tokens, `MultiWriteResponse`, 412 optimistic-lock retries) are already documented in [[concepts/zotero-api-integration-reference]].

The Windows import path has a parallel limitation. `Start-Process` on a `.ris` file feels like a headless import, but it merely hands the file to Zotero through the OS file association; Zotero then opens its import dialog and waits for a human. Two consequences follow. First, any script that "imports" this way cannot run unattended, so a truly automated ingest requires the Web API rather than the file association. Second, because the dialog's "create new collection" option is on by default, an unattended-looking import quietly routes records into a new collection rather than the intended target — precisely what happened with the 52-record Force Plate Practitioner package. The recovery chosen there is worth generalizing: when records have landed correctly but in the wrong container, renaming the container is strictly cheaper and safer than moving records or re-importing, because a re-import risks duplicate records with no compensating benefit. Finally, the linked-file caveat matters for archives whose PDFs live on Drive: Zotero indexes and references them, but does not carry copies through its own sync, so the Drive copy remains the authoritative artifact.

# Flush Pipeline Failure on Session Limit Exhaustion

On 2026-09-27 the memory-compiler flush pipeline failed repeatedly with `FLUSH_ERROR: ResultError: Claude Code returned an error result: You've hit your session limit · resets 10:50pm (America/Chicago) (exit code: 1)`. The failures began at 20:22 and continued past 21:10, following roughly 170 successful `FLUSH_OK` invocations earlier the same evening. This is a distinct failure mode from the 2026-06-13 version-skew outage: the flush machinery was intact, but the account-level quota it consumes was exhausted.

## Key Points

- **The error is a quota signal, not a defect.** `You've hit your session limit` with a named reset time identifies an account-level usage cap; there is no configuration, dependency, or path to repair, and the failure clears on its own at the reset.
- **It is distinguishable from version skew by the message, not the exit code.** Both produce `FLUSH_ERROR` and exit code 1; only the error text separates a stale bundled CLI (a real defect requiring `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk`) from quota exhaustion (requiring nothing).
- **The flush stage retries on every hook firing, so one exhausted quota yields dozens of identical log entries.** Roughly 60 `FLUSH_ERROR` entries were written across ~50 minutes, each consuming a spawn attempt that could not succeed.
- **High flush volume precedes the wall.** Approximately 170 `FLUSH_OK` entries were logged between 18:55 and 20:21 — a per-turn firing rate that consumes quota steadily even when every flush concludes there is nothing to save.
- **The day's one substantive session flushed after the reset.** The 23:47 flush, containing the Force Plate Practitioner archive record, succeeded — so the outage cost log volume and redundancy rather than the day's actual content.

## Details

The operational value of this episode is diagnostic triage. `FLUSH_ERROR` is a single label covering at least two unrelated conditions with opposite correct responses. Version skew, documented in [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]], is a genuine defect: the venv's bundled Claude Code CLI has fallen behind the system version and can no longer parse `settings.json`, every invocation fails, and the condition persists indefinitely until the SDK is re-synced. Quota exhaustion is the opposite: nothing is broken, no action helps, and the condition resolves at a stated wall-clock time. The distinguishing evidence is the error text, since both surface as exit code 1 — the same ambiguity already noted for background-task notifications in [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]], where the exit code alone cannot separate a real failure from a benign one. A stack-doctor pass triggered by the sheer count of errors would waste effort if it assumed skew; reading the message first is the cheap check.

The secondary observation concerns volume. About 170 flushes fired in the ~85 minutes before the wall, every one of them returning `FLUSH_OK` — the flush stage correctly determining there was nothing durable to record. Each still costs a spawned Claude Code invocation against the same quota the substantive work draws on, which means a high-turn-rate evening of low-value sessions can consume the budget that a genuinely productive later session needs. The failure is therefore partly self-inflicted by the pipeline's own firing cadence rather than purely external. In this instance the cost stayed low, because the day's only content-bearing session flushed at 23:47 after the 22:50 reset and was captured intact; the ~230 wasted entries bloat the daily log without deleting anything. The follow-up recorded was a stack-doctor check, which remains reasonable — not to fix the quota error, but to consider whether the flush trigger should back off after an error of this class instead of retrying on every subsequent turn until the reset arrives.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] — The flush architecture and the other major `FLUSH_ERROR` cause (claude-agent-sdk version skew), which this failure mode must be distinguished from before any repair is attempted.
- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The three-tier model in which a Tier C flush outage leaves Tier A and Tier B capture unaffected.
- [[connections/memory-compiler-tier-independence-under-failure]] — Prior empirical evidence that Tier B transcript capture survives a complete Tier C failure, which bounds the damage of an outage like this one.
- [[concepts/flush-selective-retention-nonworking-sessions]] — The retention judgment the flush stage applies when it does run; the ~170 `FLUSH_OK` results here are the default-discard end of that same decision.
- [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]] — The scheduled stack-doctor pass flagged as the follow-up for investigating the error cluster.
- [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]] — The same interpretive trap: an exit code of 1 that does not, by itself, identify what went wrong.

# Course Extraction: Three-Artifact Per-Lesson Convention

Courses extracted for the professional-development archive follow a fixed per-lesson deliverable: an MP4, a checked transcript, and a summary — three artifacts per lesson, all written into a single output folder dedicated to that course. The convention was stated explicitly on 2026-09-25 during the Sprint Biomechanics run, generalizing the Sportsmith On-Field RTP pipeline, and was applied at scale on 2026-09-27 to the 76-lesson Force Plate Practitioner course.

## Key Points

- **Three artifacts per lesson:** MP4 (the media), a checked transcript (an ASR pass reconciled against vendor captions where captions exist), and a summary. A lesson is not done until all three exist.
- **One output folder per course**, with the course's supplementary materials — PDFs, saved articles, a resource catalog — landing in the same place rather than being split across locations.
- **The contract and the inventory are declared before fan-out**, so the expected file count is known in advance and completion becomes arithmetic: 76 lessons × 3 = 228 files, verified against what is on disk.
- **"Checked" has a stated boundary.** The label claims caption-vs-ASR comparison only; it does not claim a manual audio review, and summary claims and cited studies are not independently validated.
- **The convention scales without modification.** It held from a five-part course to a 76-lesson, 14-section course, which is the evidence that it is a standing convention rather than a per-course arrangement.

## Details

The convention exists to make batch extraction verifiable. A course arrives as an opaque pile of lessons of unknown count and heterogeneous form; without a fixed per-item deliverable, "is this course archived?" has no crisp answer and partial completion is invisible. Declaring the contract up front converts the question into two countable checks — does every lesson have three files, and does the lesson count match the inventory taken before the run — which is exactly the property that made the Force Plate Practitioner close-out possible at 228 files. It also supplies a progress denominator mid-run, addressing the status-legibility gap documented in [[concepts/agent-file-status-and-path-reporting]]: "how are you doing on this?" is answerable as a fraction only when the total is fixed beforehand.

The "checked" transcript is the convention's most load-bearing and most frequently misread element. It denotes a specific, bounded procedure — generate an independent ASR transcript, diff it against the site's own captions, and keep the residue that survives comparison — not a human-verified document. Two independent derivations of the same audio have different error profiles, so their disagreements localize uncertainty; but where both agree on an error, or where neither source resolves a term, the check is silent. This is why the On-Field RTP run flagged an unresolved injury term rather than guessing, and why the Force Plate Practitioner close-out restated the scope caveat alongside the delivery count. The summary, by contrast, carries no verification at all: its claims and its cited studies were explicitly not validated. Stating both boundaries at delivery time is what keeps a large completion claim from overstating what the archive guarantees — the same discipline applied to deliverables elsewhere, where the strength of a claim is graded rather than asserted.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/force-plate-practitioner-course-archive]] — The largest application: 76 lessons, 228 files, 14 sections, delivered with the QA caveat restated.
- [[concepts/wistia-course-video-extraction]] — The earlier extraction that established machine transcripts as drafts, motivating the "checked" step.
- [[connections/cross-check-two-independent-extractions]] — The general verification move that the checked transcript instantiates.

# Connection: Rename the Container Rather Than Re-Run the Import

## The Connection

When a batch operation produces correct records under a wrong label, two repairs are available: change the label, or redo the operation so the records arrive correctly named. The 2026-09-27 Zotero import took the first path — 52 records had landed in an auto-created collection instead of `APC_JumpsCourse`, and the collection was renamed to "Force Plate Practitioner" rather than moved or re-imported. The Fireflies batch-rename workflow is the same move applied continuously: meetings whose content is fine but whose timestamp titles are unnavigable get retitled in place, never re-recorded.

## Key Insight

The cheap repair is available precisely because the expensive part of the operation already succeeded. Ingestion — pulling 52 records with attachments, or capturing a meeting's audio and gist — is the costly, error-prone, non-idempotent step; naming is metadata. Re-running ingestion to fix a name pays the full cost again *and* introduces a new failure mode the original run did not have: duplicate records, which are strictly worse than a badly named collection because they corrupt counts and require their own cleanup pass. So the repair asymmetry is not merely about effort. Redoing the work can leave the library in a worse state than the defect being fixed.

The corollary is a diagnostic question to ask before any re-run: *is the defect in the payload or in the pointer?* If the records themselves are right, the operation does not need to be repeated — only the reference to them needs correcting. The Zotero case sharpens this because the naive instinct (uncheck "create new collection," re-import into the intended one) is both more work and actively harmful. This is also why the Force Plate Practitioner close-out verified item count, PDF hashes, and a connector read *after* the rename: the check confirms the payload is intact, which is what licenses leaving it in place.

## Evidence

- **Zotero, 2026-09-27:** the RIS import dialog's default "create new collection" checkbox routed 52 records into an unintended collection. The explicit decision was to keep items where they were and rename, with duplicate-record avoidance given as the reason; the rename then succeeded programmatically once Zotero crossed into v10's writable local API.
- **Fireflies, 2026-06-17 onward:** generic timestamp-titled meetings are retitled through the API after a propose-and-confirm step. The recordings and transcripts are untouched — only the title changes — and re-recording was never a considered option.
- **Stale-cache counterpoint:** the Fireflies workflow's known hazard is the mirror image — the local cache reporting already-renamed meetings as generic — which is a case where the pointer is stale and the payload is fine, again resolved by re-syncing the reference rather than redoing the capture.

- [[concepts/fireflies-batch-rename-workflow]] — The same repair as a standing workflow: fix labels in place, never re-capture.
- [[concepts/google-drive-cleanup-antigravity]] — The adjacent conservatism: quarantine and rename-proposal staging rather than destructive re-creation.
